lead: In a building the slab and its beams are cast together, so near midspan the slab works as a wide compression flange on top of the beam. A beam with slab on both sides is a T-beam; an edge beam with slab on one side is an L-beam. The flange gives so much compression area that the neutral axis usually stays inside it. The design asks how wide the flange is, where the neutral axis lies and how much steel balances the compression.
prereq: You need the stress block and the moment equations of singly reinforced beams.

blocks.text: The slab is stressed most next to the web (shear lag), so the code uses a uniform stress over an effective width b<sub>f</sub>. b<sub>w</sub> is the web breadth, D<sub>f</sub> the slab thickness and L<sub>0</sub> the distance between points of zero moment (the span of a simply supported beam, about 0.7 times the span of a continuous one).

head: Beam
Effective flange width b<sub>f</sub>
rows: L<sub>0</sub>/(L<sub>0</sub>/b + 4) + b<sub>w</sub>, with b the actual flange width

blocks.text: b<sub>f</sub> may not exceed the web plus half the clear distance to the next beam on each side. Over a continuous support the slab is in tension and the section is a rectangle b<sub>w</sub> wide.

If M<sub>u</sub> ≤ M<sub>f</sub> = 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b<sub>f</sub> D<sub>f</sub> (d − 0.42 D<sub>f</sub>), the neutral axis lies in the flange and the beam is designed as a rectangle of width b<sub>f</sub>:
M<sub>u</sub> = 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b<sub>f</sub> x<sub>u</sub> (d − 0.42 x<sub>u</sub>)     A<sub>st</sub> = 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b<sub>f</sub> x<sub>u</sub> / (0.87 f<sub>y</sub>)
blocks.where: For an analysis, compare T = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>st</sub> with 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b<sub>f</sub> D<sub>f</sub>: if T is smaller, x<sub>u</sub> = T/(0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b<sub>f</sub>) lies in the flange.

blocks.text: Most floor T-beams fall in this case; minimum steel is 0.85 b<sub>w</sub> d/f<sub>y</sub>.

sections.h3: Neutral axis in the web (IS 456 Annex G-2.2)

blocks.text: If x<sub>u</sub> > D<sub>f</sub>, split the compression into the web (width b<sub>w</sub>, usual block) and the overhangs (width b<sub>f</sub> − b<sub>w</sub>). The top 3/7 of the compression depth is on the flat part of the curve at 0.45 f<sub>ck</sub>. If the slab lies within it (D<sub>f</sub> ≤ 3/7 x<sub>u</sub>) the overhangs carry 0.45 f<sub>ck</sub> over their full depth; otherwise the code uses y<sub>f</sub> = 0.15 x<sub>u</sub> + 0.65 D<sub>f</sub>, not more than D<sub>f</sub>.

C<sub>w</sub> = 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b<sub>w</sub> x<sub>u</sub>     C<sub>f</sub> = 0.45 f<sub>ck</sub> (b<sub>f</sub> − b<sub>w</sub>) y<sub>f</sub>     0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>st</sub> = C<sub>w</sub> + C<sub>f</sub>
blocks.where: y<sub>f</sub> = D<sub>f</sub> when D<sub>f</sub> ≤ 3/7 x<sub>u</sub>, otherwise y<sub>f</sub> = 0.15 x<sub>u</sub> + 0.65 D<sub>f</sub> ≤ D<sub>f</sub>. C<sub>w</sub> acts 0.42 x<sub>u</sub> below the top, C<sub>f</sub> at y<sub>f</sub>/2.
With xu = xu,max this gives the limiting moment of the T-beam, Mu,lim,T. If Mu exceeds it, compression steel is added as for doubly reinforced beams.

items: Find b<sub>f</sub> (formula and spacing limit, the smaller).
Compare T or M<sub>u</sub> with the flange alone at x<sub>u</sub> = D<sub>f</sub>.

If not enough, solve C<sub>w</sub> + C<sub>f</sub> = T with y<sub>f</sub> = D<sub>f</sub>; if D<sub>f</sub> > 3/7 x<sub>u</sub>, solve again with y<sub>f</sub> = 0.15 x<sub>u</sub> + 0.65 D<sub>f</sub>.
Check xu ≤ xu,max, find Mu, and check the deflection with kf.

examples.question: Floor beams of a hall are at 3.0 m centres, simply supported over an effective span of 7 m. Each has a web 300 mm wide, an effective depth of 550 mm and a monolithic slab 120 mm thick. It carries a factored moment of 400 kN·m. M25, Fe415. Find the effective flange width and the tension steel.
steps: Flange moment: M<sub>f</sub> = 0.36 × 25 × 2186 × 120 × (550 − 0.42 × 120) = 2 360 880 × 499.6 = 1179.5 kN·m. M<sub>u</sub> = 400 kN·m is far less, so the neutral axis is in the flange.

Rectangle 2186 mm wide: 400 × 10⁶ = 0.36 × 25 × 2186 × x<sub>u</sub> × (550 − 0.42 x<sub>u</sub>), that is 8263 x<sub>u</sub>² − 10 820 700 x<sub>u</sub> + 400 × 10⁶ = 0, so x<sub>u</sub> = 38.1 mm (< 120 mm).
Provide 2 bars of 28 mm + 2 bars of 25 mm (1231.5 + 981.7 = 2213 mm²) in one layer: clear gaps (300 − 60 − 16 − 106)/3 = 39 mm, more than 28 mm.
examples.answer: b<sub>f</sub> = 2186 mm; x<sub>u</sub> = 38.1 mm lies in the 120 mm slab; A<sub>st</sub> = 2075 mm², provided as 2 of 28 mm + 2 of 25 mm (2213 mm²).

examples.question: A T-beam has b<sub>f</sub> = 1000 mm, D<sub>f</sub> = 100 mm, b<sub>w</sub> = 300 mm and d = 500 mm, with 6 bars of 25 mm in tension. M20, Fe415. Find its moment of resistance.
steps: A<sub>st</sub> = 2945.2 mm². T = 0.87 × 415 × 2945.2 = 1063.4 kN. The flange alone at x<sub>u</sub> = D<sub>f</sub> gives 0.36 × 20 × 1000 × 100 = 720 kN < T, so the neutral axis is in the web.

Try y<sub>f</sub> = D<sub>f</sub>: 0.36 × 20 × 300 × x<sub>u</sub> + 0.45 × 20 × 700 × 100 = 1 063 400, so 2160 x<sub>u</sub> = 433 400 and x<sub>u</sub> = 200.6 mm. But 3/7 × 200.6 = 86.0 mm < D<sub>f</sub> = 100 mm, so the slab is thicker than the flat zone and y<sub>f</sub> must be used.
x<sub>u,max</sub> = 0.48 × 500 = 240 mm, so x<sub>u</sub> < x<sub>u,max</sub>: under-reinforced.
examples.answer: Neutral axis in the web, x<sub>u</sub> = 210.6 mm, y<sub>f</sub> = 96.6 mm; M<sub>u</sub> = 462.1 kN·m, below the T-beam limit of 490.4 kN·m.

traps: Writing b<sub>f</sub> = L<sub>0</sub>/6 + b<sub>w</sub> + 2Df. The code term is 6Df for a T-beam and 3Df for an L-beam; with 2Df the first example would get b<sub>f</sub> = 1707 mm instead of 2187 mm.
Treating a beam with the neutral axis in the web as a rectangle b<sub>f</sub> wide: in the second example that gives x<sub>u</sub> = 147.7 mm, outside the flange it assumes.
Using 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> for the flange overhangs. They lie in the flat part of the stress curve and carry 0.45 f<sub>ck</sub>.
Counting the web twice: the overhang width is b<sub>f</sub> − b<sub>w</sub>, not b<sub>f</sub>.

quiz.q: Write the IS 456 effective flange width of a T-beam and of an L-beam.
quiz.a: T-beam: L<sub>0</sub>/6 + b<sub>w</sub> + 6Df. L-beam: L<sub>0</sub>/12 + b<sub>w</sub> + 3Df. Neither may exceed the web plus half the clear distance to the next beam on each side.

quiz.q: Why is the whole slab width not used as the flange?
quiz.a: Compression spreads into the slab through shear, so the stress falls away from the web (shear lag); the effective width carries the same force at a uniform stress.

quiz.q: b<sub>w</sub> = 300 mm, D<sub>f</sub> = 100 mm, L<sub>0</sub> = 6000 mm, clear distance to the beams on each side 2700 mm. Find b<sub>f</sub>.
A T-beam has b<sub>f</sub> = 1500 mm, D<sub>f</sub> = 120 mm, d = 500 mm, M25, Fe415 and 4 bars of 25 mm. Where is the neutral axis?
In worked example 2, why was the first trial x<sub>u</sub> = 200.6 mm rejected?
quiz.a: It assumed the whole 100 mm slab was at 0.45 f<sub>ck</sub>, which needs D<sub>f</sub> ≤ 3/7 x<sub>u</sub> = 86.0 mm. It is not, so y<sub>f</sub> = 0.15 x<sub>u</sub> + 0.65 D<sub>f</sub> must be used, giving x<sub>u</sub> = 210.6 mm.

beyond: Not for the exam. Box-girder bridge decks show shear lag on a larger scale, and bridge codes give effective widths that vary along the span. Search for shear lag in box girders.

figure.caption: The T-beam of the second worked example: the steel needs more compression than the 100 mm slab can give, so the neutral axis drops to 210.6 mm in the web; the overhangs carry 0.45f<sub>ck</sub> over the equivalent depth y<sub>f</sub> = 96.6 mm and the web carries the usual block.
